entities.name: Giovanni da Verrazzano
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Giovanni da Verrazzano, an Italian mariner from the Republic of Florence, carved a significant, albeit often overlooked, path in the early Age of Exploration by undertaking the first documented European voyage along the eastern seaboard of North America in 1524. Operating under the patronage of King Francis I of France, Verrazzano's expedition aimed to discover a Northwest Passage to Asia, thereby challenging the established dominance of Spain and Portugal in the New World. His meticulous charting of the coastline from present-day North Carolina to Newfoundland provided France with an early claim to vast territories and fundamentally reshaped European understanding of the North American continent's geography.

Verrazzano embarked from France in January 1524 aboard La Dauphine, sailing westward to reach the American coast near what is now Cape Fear, North Carolina. Over the ensuing months, he meticulously explored and mapped approximately 3,000 kilometers of coastline, becoming the first European to enter what is now New York Harbor, which he named 'Angoulême' in honor of the French king. His observations included detailed descriptions of the indigenous peoples encountered, such as the Wampanoag in Narragansett Bay (which he called 'Refugio'), and the extensive coastal topography, noting the barrier islands and the distinct lack of any obvious passage to the Pacific.
